body:
Extend post and machine support to the secondary **Laguna Swift** and **Grizzly** CNC router controllers identified in #1907 research, after the RichAuto DSP A11 slice proves on hardware.

## Scope (OEM manuals only)

1. **WinCNC** (earlier Laguna `MCNC Swift` models):
   - Supports `.tap`/`.nc`, square-bracket comments `[...]`, `G20` / `G21` (note `G22` in older manuals), `G91.1`, `L91`, `G53` machine coordinates, `G4 X<sec>` dwell in seconds, `G81`/`G83`, `G43` + `M37` macros, and scripted `M6`.
2. **DSP-J2** (`Grizzly G0403` benchtop):
   - Requires plain **ANSI** text (no UTF-8 BOM) on FAT16/FAT32 USB drives, `G20`/`G21`, `G00`-`G03`, `M03`-`M05`, manual `M6` lift, and expanded plain-move drilling.
3. **RichAuto DSP B18 4-axis** (`Grizzly G0932`):
   - Same core RichAuto dialect as A11 plus 4th rotary `C` axis (`51-3/16"` x `98-7/16"` x `7-7/8"` Z, `7-7/8"` C swing, 472 IPM C rapid, 4 HP 0-18,000 RPM stated, ER25).
4. **Siemens Sinumerik 808D Advanced** (`Grizzly G0934` 5' x 10' 8-pos rotary ATC):
   - Evaluate and adapt `assets/posts/sinumerik.cps` for `808D Advanced` native Siemens mode (`G290`, `CYCLE81`-`CYCLE84`) vs ISO dialect mode (`G291`, `G81`) and `.MPF` USB loading (`59-1/16"` x `118-1/8"` x `7-7/8"` Z, 12 HP 0-24,000 RPM, ER32).

## Order

Hold implementation behind the `RichAuto DSP A11` post, machine files, and test-cut kit so real hardware feedback stabilizes our shop-router baseline first.

## Done means

- Each target controller has documented OEM dialect rules and either its own `.cps` post or verified support in an existing post with conformance goldens.
- Machine `.mch` definitions pass `crates/app/tests/machine.rs` and map to their matching posts in `crates/app/src/posting.rs`.

body:
Add a built-in 3-axis router post for the **RichAuto DSP A11** controller in `assets/posts/richauto.cps`. Register it in `BUILTINS` in `crates/app/src/posting.rs` and pin it in `crates/app/tests/conformance.rs`.

## Context

Issue #1907 confirmed that mkinney's friend runs a **RichAuto DSP A11** handheld controller. Common Laguna Swift (`4x4`, `4x8`, `5x10`) and Grizzly CNC routers (`G0894`, `G0931`, `G0895`) also use this controller.

CamCraft's existing posts (`assets/posts/grblhal.cps`, `fanuc.cps`, `carvera.cps`, `tinyg.cps`) do not run safely on a RichAuto A11:
- `grblhal.cps` emits `G91.1`, `G94`, `G53 G0 Z...`, `T<n> M6`, and canned cycles. RichAuto A11 uses the pendant `AbsCntr` menu switch (`Off` = incremental) instead of `G91.1`, and basic router firmware can reject canned cycles or `G91.1`.
- `fanuc.cps` emits `%`, `O0001`, `T.. M6`, `G43 H..`, `G49`, `G91 G28 Z0`, and `G84` tapping.

## Specification (OEM manuals only)

1. **Units and file format:** default to `mm` (`G21`) to match RichAuto's internal metric math and avoid `G20` scale errors. Write `.nc` ASCII files with parentheses comments `(...)`. Omit `%`, `O` program numbers, and `;` comments.
2. **Preamble and arcs:** write `G21`, `G90`, `G17`, `G40`, and `G80`. Omit `G91.1`, `G94`, `G43`, and `G49`. Emit incremental `I`/`J`/`K` matching `AbsCntr = Off`. Handle `G54` cleanly (`G54` default or document `Read G54` vs `Ign G54` in post notes; handle or refuse multi-WCS safely).
3. **Spindle and warm-up:** write `S<rpm> M3`. Add a configurable spindle dwell property (`G04 P<ms>`, default `0`) so the post works alongside the pendant `Spindle Delay` setting. Document 8-step `S1`-`S8` VFD wiring in post comments.
4. **Drilling and tool changes:** expand all canned drill cycles (`G81`, `G82`, `G83`, `G73`, `G86`, `G89`) to plain `G0`/`G1` moves (using the pattern in `assets/posts/carvera.cps` and `tinyg.cps`). Refuse mid-program tool changes on the initial 3-axis manual slice (or lift Z cleanly and write `M0` with `(CHANGE TOOL T<n>)` rather than bare `T<n> M6`).
5. **Refusals and footer:** refuse `G84` tapping, `G41`/`G42` cutter compensation, and probing. Retract Z to clearance height in work coordinates, stop spindle (`M5`) and coolant (`M9` if active), and end with `M30` (no trailing `%`).

## Rules

- Clean room: use only RichAuto DSP A11 OEM documentation, RS-274 / ISO 6983 standards, and CamCraft repository patterns (`assets/posts/AGENTS.md`). Do not read or copy Autodesk, HSMWorks, or third-party CAM posts.

## Done means

- `assets/posts/richauto.cps` exists and registers in `BUILTINS` in `crates/app/src/posting.rs`.
- `crates/app/tests/conformance.rs` passes for `RichAuto DSP A11` across all mill goldens and refuses `G84`, `G41`/`G42`, and probing by name.
- Posted `.nc` output uses `G21`, incremental `I`/`J`, expanded drilling moves, `(...)` comments, safe Z retract, and `M30` with no `%`, `O` headers, `G91.1`, `G43`, or `G49`.
- Decision entry added under `docs/decisions/`.

**The request (mkinney, 2026-11-15):** "My friend has a table like that. It's similar to Laguna Swift or Grizzly. Can you open a research only issue to research Laguna and Grizzly CNC machines? I can probably have him do test cuts."

**Research, not code.** Pick never takes this issue. It is answered in comments, then broken into sub-issues (AGENTS.md "needs-research"). A real machine is available through mkinney for test cuts. The exact model and controller of the friend's machine are still to be confirmed (open question 1).

## Why

CamCraft has machine files and posts for hobby routers (Sienci AltMill/grblHAL, Makera Carvera, TinyG, Tormach 24R) but none for the Laguna or Grizzly CNC router lines. These are common full-size shop routers (4x4 and 4x8 tables). Their controllers and G-code differ from LinuxCNC/PathPilot.

## Open questions

1. **The friend's machine:** make, model, table size, spindle (power, rpm range, collet), the tool changer (manual, or ATC on some Swift models), and the CONTROLLER. Ask for a photo of the controller or pendant and of its "about" or version screen.
2. **Controllers in these lines** (from public documentation only): which controllers each Laguna Swift and Grizzly CNC model ships with (for example a handheld DSP controller, Mach3/Mach4, UCCNC, or a maker-specific controller). For each one: the G-code dialect, supported G/M codes, arcs (I/J, R, the plane), canned cycles, work offsets, tool length offsets, units, the line-number and comment rules, and the file size and transfer limits (USB, line length).
3. **Machine data for a machine file:** X/Y/Z travel, max feeds and rapids, spindle range, the tool change position, and the origin conventions (the corner, Z0 at the table or the stock top).
4. **Post needs:** what our generic posts already produce that would run, and what must differ (the preamble, the spindle start and warm-up, M6 and tool change handling, the end of program, safe Z).
5. **Work flow:** how the operator sets the work zero, touches off tools (a Z puck or a fixed sensor), and loads files.
6. **Test-cut plan:** a short, safe set of test programs for the friend's machine, made with CamCraft: an air cut first, then foam or MDF. What to measure and report (the controller accepts the file, arcs are correct, the scale is correct, the tool change behaves).

## Clean-room rules

- **Used:** Laguna's and Grizzly's public documentation (manuals, spec sheets, published support articles), the controller makers' public manuals, general CNC knowledge, and the friend's own test results.
- **Not used:** any Autodesk Fusion or HSMWorks post or output, and third-party CAM post processors (Fusion, Vectric VCarve/Aspire, others) for these machines. Do not copy text from manuals. Cite and summarise only.

## Sub-issues to file (when the research is done)

- Machine file(s) for the friend's model (and the common sizes of the line).
- A post for the controller, or a variant of an existing post, with goldens.
- A test-cut kit for the friend (the programs plus a one-page check sheet). The results come back via mkinney.
- A docs section: the router first part (with the AltMill/grblHAL page).

**Done means:** every open question has an answered comment, the friend's controller is confirmed, the sub-issues are filed with "Part of #this", and this umbrella is closed.

title: Turning thread: flank passes end short of the G76 end point that the control runs to

labels.name: area:turning

labels.name: P7
labels.description: Owed polish and small fixes

body:
Found during #1842.

## What happens

With "Threading: G76 cycle" and a flank infeed, the Fanuc lathe post writes one G76 cycle. Two published manuals show that the control ends every pass at the programmed end point D:

- FANUC Series 0i-F lathe operator's manual B-64604EN-1, section 4.2.7, Fig. 4.2.7 (a).
- Siemens SINUMERIK ISO Turning programming manual A5E52211627B, Fig. 4-25.

The turning kernel (`crates/motion/src/turning/thread.rs`, the pass loop) shifts the start AND the end of each pass by the same flank offset. Thus a shallower pass ends short of D by `(k - depth) * tan(a/2)`. Only the root pass ends at D.

## Effect

The control cuts each shallower pass a little longer than the laid pass that the verdict and the stock simulation see. The extra length is at a smaller depth, inside the groove that the root pass cuts to D. It removes no material beyond the root pass and does not move toward a shoulder. Thus this is not a wrong-output defect. But the simulated passes are not exactly the passes that run.

`crates/app/tests/lathe_post_g76_sources.rs::every_pass_runs_to_the_posted_end_z_inside_the_root_pass` pins the present difference.

## Done means

One of these:

- The kernel lays each flank pass of a G76-postable plan to the same end station, and the pin changes to assert that.
- Or a decision records why the present laid ends stay.

**The request (mkinney, 2026-11-15):** "Do we need to handle svg file import?" ... "Yes file it". Many waterjet, laser and plasma users draw in Inkscape or Illustrator and export SVG. WAZER's own app takes SVG and DXF (see #1525).

## What

Import an SVG file as 2D sketch geometry for 2D operations (Contour, Pocket, Engrave/Trace, plasma or waterjet profile). It goes into the same sketch entity as the DXF import, so the operations need no new input path.

## Depends on

- #1860 (DXF core reader), #1861 (2D sketch chaining, outer-vs-hole nesting, open chains) and #1862 (the sketch ECS entity, .camproj persistence, undoable import).
- Stack on those: the SVG reader only produces sketch chains and reuses chaining, nesting and the import command.

## Scope

- **Elements:** `path` (M/L/H/V/C/S/Q/T/A/Z, absolute and relative), `line`, `polyline`, `polygon`, `rect` (with rx/ry), `circle`, `ellipse`. `g` groups with `transform` (matrix, translate, scale, rotate, skew), applied to the geometry.
- **Curves:** cubic and quadratic Béziers and elliptical arcs become arcs or polylines within the document's chord tolerance. An arc stays an arc where it is circular after the transform.
- **Units and scale:** `width`/`height` with units (mm, cm, in, pt, pc, px), and the `viewBox`. px uses 96 px/in (the CSS rule). If the file states no physical size, the import asks for the scale. It never guesses silently.
- **Y axis:** SVG Y points down. Flip it so the drawing appears as it does in the editor.
- **Ignored, with a note:** fill, stroke style, text (unless converted to paths), images, clip paths, masks, `use` references to symbols outside the file.
- **Refusals, by name:** a malformed path, a zero or negative size, a degenerate arc, and a file larger than the import budget give a clear error, never a panic (the Prime Directive).
- **MCP:** an `import_svg` tool, or the shared sketch-import tool with format svg (AGENTS.md "Commands ship with an MCP tool").

## Not in scope (later)

- Text to outlines (fonts), embedded images, and CSS stylesheets.

## Done means

- A fixture SVG set (a rectangle with a hole, Bézier and arc shapes, a nested group with transforms, mm and in documents, and one file without a physical size) imports to the expected sketch chains. The tests pin the chain count, closure, nesting and size within tolerance.
- A 2D Contour on an imported SVG posts. A golden is pinned for one plasma or waterjet-style profile.
- Malformed fixtures are refused by name and never panic. The importer fuzz test covers the SVG reader.
- The user guide import page (and #1525's waterjet notes) lists SVG.

body:
Maintainer request from #1452 ("We should be able to load DXF file to do profile cuts on.").

## Goal
Build a clean-room ASCII DXF reader in `crates/geometry/src/dxf/`. Read Autodesk's published DXF Reference only. Add zero new external crate dependencies. Keep the API neutral so #743 and #744 can share it later.

## Scope
- Parse DXF sections `HEADER`, `TABLES`, and `ENTITIES`.
- Read `$INSUNITS` explicitly as `Known(Unit)` (inch code `1`, millimeter code `4`, plus standard length scales), `MissingOrUnitless` (`0` or absent), or `Unsupported(i32)`. Never guess millimeters vs inches on missing units.
- Read `LAYER` definitions and keep layer names on every extracted primitive.
- Parse 2D primitives `LINE`, `ARC`, `CIRCLE`, `LWPOLYLINE`, and `POLYLINE`/`VERTEX`/`SEQEND`. Convert group-42 bulges into exact `Arc` segments and keep `ARC` and `CIRCLE` exact without polygonizing.
- Skip `TEXT`, `MTEXT`, `DIMENSION`, and `HATCH`, and count skipped entities per kind in an import summary struct.
- Reject non-planar extrusion vectors (`210`, `220`, `230` tilted away from `+Z`) or varying Z heights by name.
- Guard untrusted input strictly: detect and refuse Binary DXF (`AutoCAD Binary DXF`) headers, enforce maximum file size, entity count, and vertex count caps before bulk allocation, reject NaN/Inf or coordinates past `geo2d::COORD_LIMIT`, drop or refuse zero-length entities safely, and use zero `unwrap`/`expect`/`panic!`.
- Leave `SPLINE`, `ELLIPSE`, and `BLOCK`/`INSERT` to the follow-up curve/block sub-issue, refusing them by DXF entity name for now.

## Done means
Tests parse valid ASCII DXFs with rectangles, circles, arcs, bulges, layers, and `$INSUNITS` into exact primitives; tests refuse binary files, malformed group codes, truncated streams, unsupported entities, tilted extrusions, NaN values, and oversized counts by name; a deterministic smoke-fuzz test runs with zero panics.

title: 3D Pocket: the level law keeps only the flute radius off the walls, so a shank wider than the flutes or the holder touches walls taller than the flute length (op reads ok, the post is held)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area:3d
labels.description: 3D milling and finishing

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround; fix now

body:
## What happens

A 3D Pocket level keeps the cutter centre one flute radius off the material above the level. The ladder does not look at the shank or the holder. Thus, beside a wall that is taller than the flute length, a shank that is wider than the flutes touches the wall. At a larger depth the holder touches the part too.

The generator reports the op as `ok`. Verify then names each such move as `shank_hit` (part) and each lift out of such a cut as `rapid_in_stock`. All of these findings have `blocks_post: true`, and `verify` holds the post by the op (`held_by`). Thus the output is not silent, but the user gets a toolpath that cannot post.

## Evidence

The PR #1772 takeover found this (review 5910347140 of PR #1772).

- The sample `testdata/models/sample_ap214.step` as imported, stock from the model, tool `EM-0600-4FL` (6 mm, 15 mm flute, 8 mm shank, 40 mm shank length, 44 mm holder). The part is 118 mm tall. 3D Pocket `R1` gives 306 `shank_hit` and 30 `rapid_in_stock`. All 30 rapids are vertical lifts up out of a cut. There is no gouge.
- The same `R1` path (byte-identical moves) with `flute_len` 125 and `shank_d` 6 gives no findings and `ok: true`.
- A closed cavity (40 mm block, 20 x 20 mm cavity, 30 mm deep, no open side) gives 121 `shank_hit` and 6 `rapid_in_stock` with the same tool. The result is the same with the footprint law of main (before #1749) and with the law of PR #1772. Thus the defect is on main.
- #1840 reports the same kind of shank and holder findings for the 3D Finish `S1` on the same sample.
- Pin: `crates/app/tests/shared_face_bodies.rs::the_sample_as_imported_roughs_the_3d_pocket_beside_its_silhouette` asserts this reading by name.

## Workaround

Use a tool whose flutes reach the full depth, with a shank that is not wider than the flutes. Or set Bottom Z to a depth that the tool reaches.

## What to decide

One of these, by design:

1. The ladder keeps the shank radius off the material above `level + flute_len`, and the holder radius off the material above `level + flute_len + shank_len`. Then the levels that the tool cannot reach are left as rest and named.
2. The generator refuses the levels that the tool cannot reach, by name, before it builds the path.

Do not change the verify laws. They are correct.

## Done means

A whole-model 3D Pocket with a tool that cannot reach the full depth beside a tall wall gives a path that verifies with no `shank_hit` and no `rapid_in_stock`, or a refusal or warning by name at generation. The pin in `shared_face_bodies.rs` changes to assert the new reading.

title: Fanuc lathe G76: four schedule readings are unverified; a wrong Z-shift or end-Z reading moves a flank thread axially or into a shoulder

labels.name: bug

body:
## What is open

The Fanuc lathe post (`assets/posts/fanuc-lathe.cps`) can write the two-block G76 thread cycle (post option G76 cycle). The post models the control's pass schedule from public Fanuc-compatible references (GSK988TA manual, LinuxCNC G76 for the flank sign). No source that we read states four readings of that schedule. No run on a Fanuc control or on a Fanuc simulator confirms them. The PathPilot Hub simulation cannot check them, because its lathe uses the LinuxCNC one-block `G76 P.. J.. K..`.

Found in the full review of PR #517 (https://github.com/NeoTech/Camcraft/pull/517#pullrequestreview-5910390160). The readings are recorded in `docs/decisions/417-g76-matches-verified.md`.

In the table, k is the thread height and a is the tool angle of the first block (twice the flank angle).

| Item | Reading that the post uses | What a wrong reading can do | Threads affected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Z-shift sign, and which pass sits at the programmed Z | Deeper passes move in the direction of travel (LinuxCNC sign). The post sets the start Z to `c_first - k*tan(a/2)`, so pass n starts at `start + depth_n*tan(a/2)`. | The whole thread moves axially by `k*tan(a/2)` to `2k*tan(a/2)`. For the golden `thread_g76_area.nc` (2 mm lead) that is 0.6 to 1.25 mm. This is a cut in the wrong place. | Flank threads only (a not 0) |
| 2. End-Z shift | Each pass ends at the programmed end Z. | If the control also shifts the end of each pass by `depth*tan(a/2)`, the root pass ends `k*tan(a/2)` past the end Z. At a shoulder, the tool can cut into the shoulder. | Flank threads only (a not 0) |
| 3. Minimum-depth clamp | Q(dmin) is a per-pass minimum against the previous clamped depth. | The pass count or the per-pass depth changes. The root does not change. The control can cut fewer, deeper passes than the verdict judged (the tool load is not judged). | Constant-area ladders. Equal-depth ladders (the default) are not affected. |
| 4. Rounding | Words are whole least increments. R comes from the rounded ladder and is refused beyond one increment. | The pass count is fixed. Single rungs of a long sqrt ladder can differ from the laid ones by a few increments. This is not a gouge. | Long sqrt ladders |

The default radial thread (a = 0) has no Z shift. Items 1 and 2 do not change it. Main already writes the flank angle and the flank start (#416). Thus this risk is on main now. PR #517 does not add it.

## Priority

`P3`. A wrong reading of item 1 or 2 is wrong posted G-code (a `P1` class). But no source shows that the reading is wrong, and the defect is not shown. A workaround exists: the default output is the G32 chain, which does not use the control's schedule, and the default infeed is radial. If a control run shows that item 1 or 2 is wrong, raise this issue to `P1`.

## Open question (do not implement here)

Must the Fanuc post refuse, or warn, for a flank-angle G76 (a not 0) until items 1 and 2 are verified? A refusal makes the output safe now, but it removes a cycle that can be correct. A warning keeps the cycle but can be ignored. Decide this before the control run, or with its result.

## Done means

- A run on a Fanuc lathe control, or on the vendor's simulator, posts the goldens `thread_g76.nc` (mm and inch) and `thread_g76_area.nc`.
- The run records, for each pass: the start Z, the end Z and the depth.
- Each of the four items is confirmed, or the post is changed to the control's reading with a pinning test.
- `docs/decisions/417-g76-matches-verified.md` (or a new decision entry) records the result.
- The open question above has a recorded answer.

body:
What happens:
- `fanuc-lathe.cps` formats lengths with `fixed()`. This function removes the trailing zeros and also the decimal point. A whole-number length is written as `Z14`, `Z8` or `X30`, not `Z14.`.
- The Fanuc mill post does the same. Example: `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/fanuc/probe_bore_centre.nc` has `G00 Z50` and `G31 X30 Y30 Z25 F300`.
- The first-block G76 `R` word of PR #517 uses the same format. A finishing allowance of exactly 1 mm posts `R1`.

Why this is a defect:
- The published Fanuc Series 0i parameter manuals define parameter 3401 bit 0 (DPI). With DPI=0, a value with no decimal point is in the least input increment. With DPI=1 ("pocket calculator type"), it is in mm or inch.
- With DPI=0 and IS-B, `Z14` is 0.014 mm, not 14 mm. A rapid to `Z14` then goes to almost Z0. This can cause a collision.
- Other posts of this project already keep the decimal point for this reason: see the comments in `assets/posts/sinker-iso.cps` (line 53), `assets/posts/sodick-wire.cps` (line 58) and `assets/posts/AGENTS.md` (line 257).

Found during the takeover of PR #517 (lathe G76 R word). PR #517 does not cause this. Its R word follows the format of the other length words of the post.

Questions to answer:
- Which posts read the same format: fanuc, fanuc-lathe, haas, mazak, doosan-dnm, others?
- Does the project assume DPI=1? If yes, write this in each post header and in the machine documentation. If no, write each length with a decimal point (`Z14.`).

Done means: each Fanuc-family post writes a length so that the control reads the same value with DPI=0 and DPI=1, or the post header and the user documentation state the DPI=1 requirement. The goldens are updated in one commit, with a test that pins a whole-number length.

title: 3D Deburr: edge selection, ball and lollipop tools, steep edges, and a multi-axis mode

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

body:
The maintainer asked for this issue in chat on 2026-11-15: "Issue; enhancement; Operation; 3D-Debur - research online, find papers on it usingg perplexity, document it as an issue."

This issue records the research. It also lists the work that the 3D Deburr operation needs to become a full edge-break operation. An agent filed it for the maintainer.

## What we have today

The Deburr operation exists (`crates/motion/src/finishing3d/deburr.rs`, `OpParams::Deburr`). It does this:

- It finds the edges automatically: convex creases and open rims of the mesh.
- It uses a cone tool (chamfer mill) with a vertical tool axis.
- It has one authored number, `width`. The tip depth follows: `drop = width / tan(half-angle)`.
- It does not cut steep edges. It skips an edge that climbs faster than the cone flank and writes a note (#303).
- It clips the ride to the `top_z` / `bottom_z` window.

## What is missing

1. The user cannot select edges. The user cannot exclude edges.
2. There is no filter for the edge angle. There is no filter for holes.
3. Only the cone tool works. A ball mill and a lollipop mill do not work. Tool kinds are also a subject of #895 and #896.
4. Steep and vertical edges get no edge break.
5. The break has one shape only. There is no constant-depth mode, no large chamfer in more than one pass, and no rounded edge.
6. The tool axis is always vertical. Edges under an overhang, and edges on the side of the part, are out of reach.
7. There is no setting that says what to do with a part of an edge that the tool cannot reach.

## Research

### Behaviour of a deburr strategy in other CAM systems (public documentation, behaviour only)

Sources: the Autodesk Fusion help page "Generate a Deburr toolpath" (https://help.autodesk.com/view/fusion360/ENU/?contextId=MFG-MULTI-AXIS-DEBURR), the Autodesk blog (https://www.autodesk.com/products/fusion-360/blog/deburring-autodesk-fusion-360-tutorial/) and the Cimatron help page (https://help.cimatron.com/en/2026/english/tool_path_calculation/deburring/deburring_overview.htm). No vendor text, parameter name or asset is copied here.

- The operation follows the external edges of the part and makes a chamfer or a rounded edge.
- The system finds the edges automatically, or the user selects them. The user can exclude edges.
- A minimum edge angle removes edges that are almost tangent.
- The user can exclude circular holes, with a diameter range.
- The edge break has a constant width or a constant depth. A large chamfer and a rounded edge need more than one pass.
- Ball, lollipop, flat, chamfer, tapered and spot-drill tools are permitted in Fusion. Cimatron permits ball and lollipop tools only.
- The contact point can be a fixed point along the flute.
- The operation has a 3-axis, a 4-axis and a 5-axis mode. The 3-axis mode cuts only the edges that the tool can reach from above, and it can exclude vertical edges.
- A setting controls the areas that the tool cannot reach.
- The system checks the holder for collisions. In a multi-axis mode it changes the tilt when it finds a collision.

### Papers and standards

| Subject | Source |
|---|---|
| Burr definition, burr types, edge measure, removal methods (review) | Aurich, Dornfeld, Arrazola, Franke, Leitz, Min: "Burrs - Analysis, control and removal", CIRP Annals 58(2), 519-542, 2009. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cirp.2009.09.004 (open copy: https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1sc2k1b8) |
| Edge states on a drawing: burr, sharp edge, undercut; one value "edge measure a" | ISO 13715, edges of undefined shape (editions 2000 and later). Licensed document: use the summary in the CIRP review. |
| Conference papers on burr control and removal | Aurich, Dornfeld (eds.): "Burrs - Analysis, Control and Removal", Springer, 2010. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-00568-8 |
| 3-axis ball-end path along a hole intersection curve, constant chamfer | Abele, Schützer, Güth, Meinhard: "Deburring of cross-drilled holes with ball-end cutters - modeling the tool path", Production Engineering 12, 25-33, 2018. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11740-017-0781-0 |
| Numerical 3-axis ball-end path on complex intersections, maximum ball diameter, collision avoidance | Schützer, Abele, Meinhard et al.: "Deburring of complex-shaped drilling intersections: a numerical method for modelling the tool path", Int J Adv Manuf Technol 102, 67-79, 2019. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-018-3205-1 |
| End mill, ball mill, conical and chamfer tools on 4-axis and 5-axis machines; interference and collision | Gosselin: "Gear Tooth Edge Deburring and Chamfering in 5Axis CnC Manufacturing", in Gears in Design, Production and Education, Springer, 2021, 153-184. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-73022-2_7 |
| Ball-end chamfer of a curved crest: ball centre at distance R from the two chamfer borders; axis direction in a feasible region | Wei, Li, Tan: "Tooth crest chamfering method of spiral bevel gear using ball end milling cutter", Proc IMechE Part B, 2021. https://doi.org/10.1177/0954405420949757 |
| Deburr paths from CAD edges: group the edges, make a tool pose for each edge, add approach and depart points | NIST: "CAD Directed Robotic Deburring" (https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=820241) and "An Advanced Deburring and Chamfering System" (https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=820281) |
| Position and orientation planning, deburr in layers | "A Robotic Deburring Methodology for Tool Path Planning and Process Parameter Control of a Five-Degree-of-Freedom Robot Manipulator", Applied Sciences 9(10), 2033, 2019. https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/9/10/2033 |
| Tool trajectory from a 3D scan (mesh input, no B-rep) | Onstein, Bjerkeng, Martinsen: "Automated Tool Trajectory Generation for Robotized Deburring of Cast Parts Based on 3D Scans", Procedia CIRP 118, 507-512, 2023. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procir.2023.06.087 |
| Lead angle and edge curvature change the chamfer width on a 5-axis machine | "Analysis of the Deburring Efficiency of EN-AW 7075 Aluminum Alloy ...", Materials 17(24), 6267, 2024. https://www.mdpi.com/1996-1944/17/24/6267 |

Limits of this research:

- One long research request timed out, and one request got a rate-limit error. The table comes from search results and abstracts.
- Nobody has read the full text of the papers behind a paywall. The design step must read a paper before it uses a formula from it.
- The details of other CAM systems (hyperMILL, Mastercam, SolidCAM) are not verified and are not used here.
- No source confirmed typical drawing values for an edge break.

### Geometry (our derivation from elementary geometry; the design step must check it against the papers)

Symbols: `E` is a point on a convex edge. `n1` and `n2` are the outward unit normals of the two faces. `b = (n1 + n2) / |n1 + n2|` is the bisector that points out of the material. `θ` is the angle of the material wedge. The angle between the normals is `π - θ`.

- **Edge filter.** An edge is a candidate when it is convex and the angle between the normals is not less than the minimum edge angle. The current crease test already finds convex pairs.
- **Symmetric chamfer.** A chamfer with setback `s` on each face has the width `w = 2·s·sin(θ/2)`. Its plane is perpendicular to `b`. The plane is at the depth `d = s·cos(θ/2)` below `E`.
- **Ball of radius R, centre on the bisector.** The centre is `C = E + h·b` with `h = -s·cos(θ/2) + sqrt(R² - s²·sin²(θ/2))`. The ball then cuts each face at the setback `s`. The condition is `R >= w/2`. The ball makes a concave break, not a flat chamfer. The ball centre does not depend on the tool axis, thus the same law is correct for the 3-axis mode and the multi-axis modes. For a lollipop tool, the axis must also keep the neck clear.
- **Cone tool with half-angle α.** The flank makes a flat symmetric chamfer only when the angle between the tool axis and `b` is `90° - α`. With a vertical axis, the break is symmetric only on some edges. The current ride accepts this and defines `width` in the horizontal plane of the edge.
- **Reach, 3-axis.** A ball position is legal only if the ball, the shank and the holder do not touch other faces. The existing envelope check (`verify`, `Mode::Envelope`) is the judge.

## Proposed slices (each one becomes a sub-issue)

1. Edge set: manual selection and exclusion of edges, a minimum edge angle, and a hole filter with a diameter range. Each one needs a command, a project file field, an MCP tool and a UI control.
2. Ball and lollipop tools in the 3-axis mode, with the ball-centre law above. A lollipop tool reaches a steep or vertical edge from the side.
3. Break shape: constant width or constant depth, and a larger chamfer or a rounded edge in more than one pass.
4. A setting for a part of an edge that the tool cannot reach: skip it with a note, or refuse the operation by name.
5. Multi-axis mode (4-axis and 5-axis): the tool axis tilts to reach edges, with a collision check of the holder.
6. Simulation: the edge-break records (#303, #529) must accept the new break shapes, so that the gouge check does not refuse an intended break.

Each strategy choice is a user parameter with a default. No choice is fixed in the code.

## Open questions (reason for `needs-research`)

- Does manual edge selection select mesh edge chains, or the B-rep edges of the solid model when the import has them?
- Which definition of "width" is the one setting for all tools: the chamfer width `w`, or the setback `s`?
- Is the multi-axis mode a mode of this operation, or a different operation in the multi-axis family?
- What are the default minimum edge angle and the default width?

## Safety

This work changes toolpath geometry and the gouge check, thus the safety floor applies to each sub-issue (`effort:high` or more). A break that the tool cannot make safely must be refused or skipped with a note. It must never be cut wrong.

Done means: the open questions have answers in comments, the sub-issues are filed with "Part of" this issue, and this issue is closed with a comment that names them.

Part of #1152 (and #543). Found while working #1152.

**What happens:** the size law (`sinker_undersize::judge`) judges a body electrode on the X and Y extents of its outline. An inward offset moves a sharp corner that is not square to the axes further than the undersize. For such a cavity (a diamond, a rotated rectangle) the extents that the spark gap reaches are short of the cavity's extents. **What is wanted:** the size law compares the electrode's outline with the cavity's outline, not their extents. The Sinker Burn then states the cavity's outline (today it states `cavity_x` and `cavity_y` only). A finish is refused only when a wall is left under size by more than the slack.

body:
What happens: a Circular operation with entry Ramp (helical, after PR #1663) retracts to the clearance height after every depth level, then rapids straight back down to the floor it just cut, then starts the next helix. Seen in a PathPilot Hub run on the 770MX simulator, 2026-11-14 (file `hub-tests/1663-circular-ramp/pr.nc`, PR head 8d63209a; T4 4 mm end mill; 6 mm hole, two rings r 0.0394 and r 0.0197; steps 0.0394 in):

```
G3 X-1.3386 Y0.1142 Z-0.0987 I0.0394 J0 F19.69   (last ring of the level)
G0 X-1.3386 Y0.1142 Z0.1969                       (rapid up to clearance)
G0 X-1.3386 Y0.1142 Z-0.0987                      (rapid down to the floor just cut)
G3 X-1.4066 Y0.1412 Z-0.1037 I-0.0394 J0 F19.69   (next helix starts)
```

It is safe: the moves are straight up and down at one X/Y inside the cut hole. But:
- Each level adds an air trip to the clearance height and back. That costs time on a deep hole with many levels.
- The rapid down ends exactly on the previous floor, with no gap. A rapid usually stops a small clearance above the floor, and the last part is fed.

Wanted: between depth levels of one Circular operation, either
- (a) stay at depth: the next helix continues from the end of the last ring with no retract (the material below is uncut, and the helix ramps into it), or
- (b) if a retract is kept, rapid down only to a small clearance above the previous floor (for example the operation's ramp clearance), then feed the rest.

(a) is preferred. A retract should stay only where the tool must leave the hole (the last level, or a level change that needs a lift). The ramp entry and the refusals stay unchanged. The posted G-code changes, so update the circular goldens with the reason.

Found while running the Hub check for PR #1663 (issue #1609).

Done means: a pin shows no rapid to the clearance height between levels of one Circular operation (or, with option b, no rapid that ends below the previous floor plus the clearance). The circular goldens are updated, and the stock simulation still shows no gouge.

title: Mask tests: compare a generated toolpath with its described shape

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:2d

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

labels.description: Accepted enhancement, not scheduled

body:
The maintainer asked for this in chat (2026-11-15):

> is it possible to use the cli tool to verify tool paths "visually".. we know what they should look like mathematically.. could we inspect them using rasterized tests?

> Idea is to sanity checks that changes to the motion crates actually gets implemented as described by the user

## Problem

A change to a toolpath generator is described in words in its issue (for example "the pass extends to the stock edge", "the corners are arcs", "the slot is cleared with trochoidal loops"). The tests of the change pin numbers that the author chose. No test compares the shape of the generated toolpath with the shape that the description gives. A change can pass its tests and not do what the user described.

## Proposal

Add a test helper that compares two masks on one grid:

- The expected region. The test builds it from the mathematical description (an outline, a depth, an extension).
- The swept region. The helper builds it from the tool footprint along the generated toolpath.

The helper gives these assertions:

- No overcut: no swept cell is outside the expected region, within one cell.
- Bounded leftover: the uncut area is below a stated limit, and the uncut cells are only in stated places.
- Engagement: no move cuts a width larger than the stated stepover.
- Shape laws: symmetry for a symmetric region, and no move outside the stock plus the stated extension.

When an assertion fails, the helper writes the difference mask as a PNG file into the test output folder. A person can then see where the toolpath is wrong. The test result comes from the numbers, not from an image comparison. No PNG golden is stored.

## Rules

- The helper is test code. It does not change a generator, a gouge check or a collision check.
- The helper is in the crate that owns the toolpath types (`crates/motion`), and uses the CPU rasteriser or its own grid. It does not need a GPU.
- The grid limits the precision to one cell. Exact laws (arc radius, depth, feed words) stay as numeric tests.
- A PR that changes a 2D generator in `crates/motion` adds or updates one mask test that states the described shape.

## First users

- Trochoidal slot.
- 2D Adaptive.
- The open-edge region of issue 1735 and the Slot extension of issue 1731.

Done means: the helper is in the repository with its own unit tests; the trochoidal slot and 2D Adaptive each have one mask test that fails when the generator is changed to overcut or to leave too much material (shown by a mutation check in the PR); a failed assertion writes the difference PNG; AGENTS.md "Testing" names the helper.

body:
Asked for by the maintainer (2026-11-13, in chat): "make an issue of using cadmpeg as file importer then i suppose.. we could open all common cad parts into camcraft that way."

What is missing: Model > Open reads STEP, STL, OBJ and `.sc`. A part saved in a CAD program's own format must first be exported to STEP by the user.

What cadmpeg is (from its crates.io entry, docs.rs page and `LEGAL.md`, read 2026-11-13; its source and format-support document were not read): a command-line converter and inspector for native CAD files, <https://crates.io/crates/cadmpeg>, Apache-2.0, version 0.6.12, very new (about 575 downloads).
- Reads `.sldprt`, `.f3d`, `.FCStd`, `.ipt`/`.iam`, `.3dm`, `.CATPart`, NX and Creo `.prt`, ACIS `.sat`/`.sab`, IGES, STEP, USD text.
- Writes STEP (AP203/214/242), IGES, USD, its own JSON form, and limited native writers.
- Commands: `convert`, `inspect`, `check`, `diff`, `measure`, `query`, `dump`, `formats`, `dialects`.
- Its docs say it "is not a library"; the per-format codecs are separate optional crates.
- Its legal policy forbids vendor SDKs, decompiled vendor binaries, NDA or leaked material and any circumvention of encryption or DRM; decoders come from files the analyst may hold plus public material, with a provenance declaration per decoder PR. It states it is not legal advice.

Wanted: Model > Open, the viewport drop of issue 1450 and the MCP `import_model` tool accept those formats by converting to STEP and loading the result through the existing STEP importer and the existing undoable import command (no second import path).

Open questions (research first; answers go in comments here, then sub-issues are filed):
1. Route. Recommended: an optional external tool - call `cadmpeg convert` when it is installed, and refuse by name ("install cadmpeg to open .sldprt files") when it is not. No crate is added and none of its code is bundled. The alternative, linking its codec crates, is a new dependency: it needs the maintainer's yes and a `docs/decisions/` entry, and its provenance becomes ours to answer for.
2. Format support. Read cadmpeg's format-support document and try real files (made by us in each program, or files whose terms allow it): which formats convert to a solid our STEP importer loads whole, and which lose faces or come out as surfaces only. Offer only the formats that pass.
3. Clean-room. Confirm on the record that reading a user's part geometry through a third-party tool brings no HSMWorks material into the project (CAM data stored inside a part file is never read), and that cadmpeg's byte-analysis method is not used for our own code.
4. How the tool is found (PATH, a setting), which version is the minimum, and how a missing or too-old tool is reported.
5. Browser build: no external process there; say so in the refusal.

Safety (Prime Directive):
- A conversion that drops geometry must not give a model that looks whole. Run cadmpeg's own `check`, read its exit code and report, and refuse or name what was lost; never machine a silently partial part.
- Units: the converted STEP's units are stated in the import summary; a file with no units asks, never guesses.
- Untrusted input: the external process runs with a time limit and an output-size limit, its temp files go in a fresh directory that is removed afterwards, the file path is passed as an argument (never through a shell string), and a crash, hang or garbage output gives a named error and leaves the project unchanged.
- The converted STEP then passes the STEP importer's own guards (issue 1536 and follow-ups).

Done means (for the research): the five questions answered in comments here, the tried formats listed with their results, and the sub-issues filed (each with one priority, one effort, area, "Done means" and "Part of" this issue); then `needs-research` is dropped and this issue is closed naming them.

What the published documentation of the product we reimplement describes (behaviour only, read through a search summary, not verified page by page):
- The setup's WCS orientation sets the default tool direction: pointing the WCS Z out of another face makes that setup's 3-axis toolpaths cut from that direction; the model is not turned. The operator flips the part on the machine to match.
  - https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/ENU/Fusion-CAM/files/MFG-TOOL-ORIENTATION-OVERVIEW.htm
  - https://www.autodesk.com/products/fusion-360/blog/fusion-360-wcs-tool-orientation/

Not let the WCS orient the part to Z..". Both give the same posted program for a flipped part; they differ in which control the user turns.

1. Keep Part alignment as the only way to turn a part (today). Then the WCS pane should not offer a tilt for a milling setup, or should offer "turn the part with Part alignment" at that moment, so a user coming from the reference product is led there before Generate refuses.
2. Or let a tilted setup WCS define the tool direction (generate in the WCS frame; `docs/decisions/1510-tilted-wcs.md` rated that effort:max: every generator, stock, heights, simulation and the post's rotated-offset refusal are involved).

Safety: whichever is chosen, a tilted WCS never generates a path in a frame other than the one shown; the refusal of PR 1518 stays until option 2 is complete.

- **z-level / waterline contours** on the model at a set stepdown (or scallop height), at least for steep regions;
- the tool's real shape (flat bottom, corner radius) used for the gouge offset;
- the shallow areas left to a later pass or flagged as rest.

Asked for by the user (2026-11-13, in chat): research-only issue for waterjet support, starting from the WAZER desktop waterjet the user owns. **Research, not code.** Pick never takes this issue; it is answered in comments and broken into sub-issues.

## Sources and clean-room rules

Clean-room rules for this research:
- **Used:** WAZER's public documentation (its support article on G-code and its materials and specs page; URLs below, cited, not copied), the Pro WAZER user manual (behaviour only), general abrasive-waterjet knowledge, and a behavioural analysis of the user's own job files exported by WAZER's web app (WAM). Those are about 120 programs from WAM 1.6 to 2.4, all Pro WAZER. Only their word and code usage and statistics were studied; no file is shared or committed.
- **Not used, and never to be used:** any Autodesk Fusion or HSMWorks post or output for WAZER (one exists in Autodesk's post library; it was not opened), WAM's JavaScript, and the machine's firmware.
- **Licence:** WAZER's G-code page is proprietary ("all rights reserved"). It is a published description of the dialect, not an open specification. Facts such as code numbers and meanings may be implemented; its text may not be copied.

## Findings so far

**Dialect** (WAM output, meanings as WAZER publishes them):
- **Modes:** G21 (mm) and G90 only. Moves are G0 and G1 only: **no arcs**, so curves are short segments. **No Z axis.** F is in mm/min. Dwell is `G4 S<seconds>`.
- **Jet and abrasive:** M3/M5 open and close the water, M8/M9 the abrasive.
- **Machine-specific M codes:** start and end of job (no M2/M30), the cut's bounding box (used by the machine's "check cut extents"), re-pierce time after a pause, and header metadata (WAM version, material name truncated to 20 characters, thickness, estimated time).
- **File format:** CRLF line endings, `;` comments, a fixed parameter header.
- **Origin:** top-left of the bed, Y negative toward the front. The cutting area is about 460 × 305 mm.
- **Per contour:** rapid to the pierce point, water on, abrasive on, stationary pierce dwell, straight lead-in, contour, then a short dwell, abrasive off, dwell, water off, dwell. The jet is never on during a rapid.
- **Kerf:** compensation is in the geometry (about half the published kerf), with no G41/G42.
- **Tabs** are uncut gaps (most contours are open).
- **Cut order:** inner contours first.
- **Feed:** the file's top F is the material rate for the chosen quality. The three qualities run at about 1 : 1.14 : 1.29. **Corner slowdown is written into F** in steps, down to about 0.45×.

**Machine:** kerf about 1.1 mm (0.044 in), maximum about 75 ipm; the pressure differs between the Pro and desktop models. The manual's error list includes a refusal of files generated by a much older WAM than the firmware.

**Materials and speeds:** the public page gives, per material and thickness, a cut rate and pierce time for each of the Pro and desktop machines. The published Pro rates sit near WAM's fine-to-medium rates; WAM's pierce times are often shorter than the published ones.

**Warranty and terms:** WAZER states that only WAM-generated files are approved, and that **edited or third-party-generated files void the warranty and breach its terms of service.** A community report says non-WAM files can leave uncut sections after pause and resume. Any CamCraft WAZER post must carry this warning prominently and must not claim WAZER approval.

## Open questions (answer before any sub-issue)

1. **Should CamCraft ship a WAZER post at all,** given the warranty and terms-of-service statement, or only a generic abrasive-waterjet post plus a user-supplied machine file? Decide with the maintainer.
2. **Pause and resume:** what does the firmware need for a third-party program to resume correctly (re-pierce after a pause, the bounding-box words)? Can that be learned from public docs alone?
3. **The corner-slowdown model:** derive it from public waterjet literature (taper and lag versus speed) rather than copying WAM's step table. What do the references say?
4. **Pierce data:** reuse #1521 (pierce and dwell data keyed by material and thickness), with waterjet as a process kind there?
5. **The operation:** a 2D abrasive-waterjet profile op, or a waterjet mode of the existing plasma/laser profile? Covers kerf offset in the geometry, leads on open contours, tabs as gaps, inner contours first, and arc linearisation tolerance.
6. **The machine file:** bed envelope and origin, kerf, max feed, model-specific speed tables (Pro vs desktop) and the bounding-box limit check.
7. **WAM project files (`.wzr`):** these are JSON with the source drawing and settings, undocumented. Importing them is out of scope unless WAZER documents the format; record that decision.

## Candidate sub-issues (filed only after the questions above are answered)

- Abrasive-waterjet profile operation (kerf, leads, tabs as gaps, inner-first order)
- Waterjet corner-slowdown and pierce-time model from published literature
- WAZER (Pro and desktop) machine definition and post, from the public dialect, with the warranty warning
- Waterjet process data in #1521's pierce and dwell tables

## Public references

- WAZER, "Understanding G-code": https://support.wazer.com/resources/preprocessing-temp/understanding-g-code
- WAZER materials and specs: https://wazer.com/materials/materials-specs/
- WAZER web app (WAM): https://wam.wazer.com/wazercam (a JavaScript app; no format docs without logging in)

Related: #1521 (plasma, laser and waterjet pierce and dwell data).

Done means: each open question is answered in a comment, the sub-issues are filed (one `P*`, one `effort:*`, `area:*`, `source:agent`, a Done means line and "Part of #<this>"), and this umbrella is closed with links to them.

body:
> bug; tools like plasma cutter - or laser for that matter, and prob waterjet as well. Would require piercing and dwell data.. Lasers usually have 1-4 piercing steps that can be used all or just one. just to get thru different thickness of material. Same with plasma.. piercing height, power at height, pressure of gas, movement of torch/laser head etc etc. Use perplexit to research this in a subagent and make a issue ticket from it where this types of tools getter better coverage.

(Maintainer, 2026-11-13, in chat.)

## What exists today

- Plasma only. `ToolKind::Torch` (`crates/tools/src/tools.rs`) is a kerf width plus rpm 0; it carries no cutting data. I found no laser or waterjet tool kind in `tools.rs`.
- The plasma operation (`crates/motion/src/plasma/mod.rs`, `emit.rs`; app side `crates/app/src/operation/types/plasma.rs`, `crates/app/src/project/plasma_dto.rs`; page `crates/ui/src/egui_app/plasma_page.rs`) has three optional per-operation numbers: pierce height, cut height, pierce delay. Left empty means "set by the controller" (AutoFS).
- The Tormach plasma post (`assets/posts/tormach-plasma.cps`) writes M207/M208/M209 for those three values and G16 for the pierce, and leaves volts, amps and gas to the control's own table. Nothing else (power, gas, pressure, torch motion at the pierce) can be stated anywhere.
- Related open issues: 621 (plasma research umbrella), 1447 (common-line cutting and marking), 1452 (DXF import for 2D cuts). No open issue covers pierce data; a "pierce" search finds only closed plasma work (670, 671).

## What is missing

1. Cut data lives on the operation, not on the tool, and is not keyed by material or thickness. Changing plate thickness means re-typing numbers.
2. Only one pierce, with one height and one delay. No transfer height, no puddle-jump (lift after pierce), no creep or start-speed ramp on exit, no amperage or gas on the tool.
3. Laser and waterjet have no tool kind, so there is nowhere to put multi-stage pierce data.
4. Posts have no way to say "this stage cannot be written in this dialect".

## Research summary (facts and concepts only, own words)

Plasma
- Transfer height: the low height where the arc first transfers to the plate. Pierce height: the higher height held while the arc pierces (limits spray onto the torch). Pierce delay: time held after transfer before the head moves. Cut height: stand-off while cutting. Torch height control holds a target arc voltage as a stand-in for the distance during the cut.
- Puddle jump (optional): after the pierce, lift to a percentage of pierce height for a short dwell to clear molten metal, then drop to cut height.
- Each system and consumable set has a maximum pierce thickness; thicker plate needs an edge start (the arc begins off the plate edge). Kerf comes from the cut chart.
- The maker's cut chart is the source of values (current, gas type and pressure, heights, voltage, speed). It normally sits in the control's material table; the program selects it and may override single values.

Laser
- Makers document up to four sequential pierce stages, each with its own time, power, pulse frequency, duty cycle, focus, nozzle distance, gas type and pressure; a stage with zero time is skipped. Parameters may ramp from a start to an end value inside a stage.
- Pierce kinds named by makers: ramped, pulsed (gradual), and a forceful short pierce; definitions vary by machine, so the data model must not hard-code them.
- Cooling dwell or gas blow is machine-specific; no standard length exists.
- Normal practice: the technology table (material and thickness) holds the recipe, the NC program selects the table and pierce type and may override.

Waterjet
- Methods: stationary, dynamic (moving toward the path while piercing), wiggle or circular (short oscillation), and low-pressure or pressure-ramp pierce for brittle or laminated material (glass, stone, ceramic, composites). Abrasive can be delayed after water starts, or fed first with pressure ramped up from low.
- No universal pierce time by thickness exists; it depends on material, pressure, nozzle and method, so it must be the user's value.

Control table versus program: recipes are usually in the control's table (selected by material and thickness) with the program choosing and sometimes overriding. A CAM system therefore needs both: store the recipe, then either post the selector or post explicit values, by dialect.

## Proposed data model

A cut-data record per tool, keyed by material and thickness (rows the user adds, copies and deletes):

- Cut parameters: cut height, feed, kerf; for plasma amperage, gas type and pressure, arc voltage; for laser power, frequency, duty, gas type and pressure, nozzle distance, focus; for waterjet pressure and abrasive flow.
- Pierce: an ordered list of 0 to 4 stages, every stage optional and individually enableable. Each stage has height, duration (dwell), power or pressure, frequency and duty (laser), gas and pressure, an optional ramp end value, and head motion during the pierce (none, wiggle or circular amplitude, or moving toward the path). Plasma uses one stage plus optional transfer height and puddle-jump (percent and dwell). Waterjet adds method, low-pressure value and abrasive delay.
- Pierce capacity per record: maximum pierceable thickness, and whether an edge start is allowed.
- Every number is entered by the user or copied from the maker's chart. Shipped example rows are marked "example" in the file and in the UI.

Editing: a cut-data table on the tool page (undoable commands, an MCP tool and script verb per the command law). The operation chooses a row (or "none: the machine's own table") and may override single values; overrides are commands too.

Operation behaviour: pierce at the start of the lead-in, run the stages in order (height move, dwell and head motion per stage), then the cut-height move and lead-in. The generated path carries the stages as records in the CL file so the post and the verifier read the same data.

Posts: each dialect writes the stages it can (dwell, height moves, selector codes or direct values). A stage or value the dialect cannot express makes the post refuse with a named reason, or write a visible comment line naming what was left to the control; it is never dropped silently. The Tormach post keeps M207/M208/M209 for the plasma values and refuses a multi-stage laser record.

## Safety rules

- A thickness above the tool's pierce capacity is refused, unless the operation states an edge start (then the lead-in must start off the plate, and that is verified).
- No silent default for a pierce time or height: an empty value either posts "controller's table" as an explicit, commented choice on a dialect that has one, or refuses.
- Stage values are checked at command creation (non-negative times and heights, power within 0 to 100 percent, at most four stages).
- Values are the user's and the machine maker's; shipped examples are labelled as examples and nothing was run on a real machine. Verification (stage order, pierce inside a kept part, head motion hitting a neighbour) joins the existing plasma laws.
- This changes posted output, so it is at least effort:high.

## Suggested slices

1. Tool-side cut-data record for the existing plasma torch (material and thickness rows, transfer height, puddle jump, pierce capacity), project file round-trip, undoable commands, MCP tool. The operation picks a row.
2. Plasma generation and the Tormach post use the row; refusal for thickness above capacity and the edge-start rule; laws and goldens.
3. Laser tool kind and machine kind with 1 to 4 pierce stages; CL records and a first laser post (dwell and height moves, explicit comment lines).
4. Waterjet tool kind: pierce methods, low-pressure pierce, abrasive delay; post support.
5. Docs and shipped example rows.

Slices 3 and 4 may need their own research issues for machine kinds; file them when slice 1 lands.

Done means: a plasma, laser or waterjet tool carries material and thickness keyed cut data with up to four ordered optional pierce stages; the operation uses the chosen row at the lead-in start; each post writes every stage or refuses or comments what it cannot; a too-thick plate without an edge start is refused; tests pin all of these.

Related: 621, 1447, 1452, 670, 671.

## Sources

- https://linuxcnc.org/docs/master/html/en/plasma/qtplasmac.html
- https://linuxcnc.org/docs/html/plasma/plasma-cnc-primer.html
- https://xnet.hypertherm.com/Xnet/library/download/?file=HYP104561
- https://www.hypertherm.com/resources/more-resources/articles/thick-metal-cutting-techniques/
- https://www.hypertherm.com/resources/more-resources/articles/torch-height-control-for-plasma-cutting/
- https://studylib.net/doc/25809509/amada-cnc-laser-machine-program-manual--2-
- https://www.fanuc.co.jp/en/product/catalog/pdf/cnc/FS30i-LB_0i-LFPlus(E)-03.pdf
- http://www.apasi.net/system/files/9999/2014/P338EN.pdf
- https://pdfcoffee.com/1-user-manual-hd-f-hd-fl-pdf-free.html
- https://www.omax.com/news/blog/4-piercing-methods-abrasive-waterjet-machining
- https://www.aquajet.co.uk/4-piercing-methods/
- https://digitallibrarynasampe.org/data/pdfs/s2019_pdfs/TP19--1458.pdf
- https://patents.google.com/patent/US9108297B2/en

body:
Asked for by the user (2026-11-13, in chat): "create a new issue for 'stock' soft jaws, so they can just be selected in CamCraft? We could just ask the user for dimensions, too."

## Today

The built-in **Soft jaw** workholding accessory (#789, `crates/app/src/accessory.rs`) is a plain block, `SoftJaw { width, height, thickness }`, defaulting to 6 × 2 × 0.75 in. The user types every size, and there are no bolt holes and no nest.

## What

1. **Stock soft-jaw presets** in the accessory picker (GUI, MCP and script), grouped by vise size, plus **Custom…** that asks for the dimensions. Sizes are the common machinable-blank sizes sold for Kurt-type vises: length × height × thickness, bolt-hole centres, screw size. Published catalog values (one vendor's public listings, 2026-11-13; generic sizes, no vendor names in the product):

   | Vise | L × H × T (in) | Bolt centres (in) | Screw |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | 4" | 4 × 2 × 1 | 2.500 | 3/8 |
   | 4" | 4 × 1.5 × 1 | – | – |
   | 5" | 5.2 × 2 × 1 | 3.125 | 3/8 or M10 |
   | 6" | 6 × 2 × 0.75 | 3.875 | 1/2 or M12 |
   | 6" | 6 × 2 × 1 | 3.875 | 1/2 or M12 |
   | 6" | 6 × 2 × 1.5 | 3.875 | 1/2 or M12 |
   | 6" | 6 × 2.5 × 1 | 3.875 | 1/2 or M12 |
   | 8" | 8 × 3 × 1 | 4.750 | 5/8 |
   | 8" | 8 × 3 × 1.5 | 4.750 | 5/8 |

   A dash means not published; hole height from the bottom and the counterbore size are not published for any size. Presets are a convenience list in a data file the user can extend, not a vendor catalog. Units follow the document. Material is a choice (aluminum or steel), for the sim and for feeds.

2. **Bolt holes in the jaw model:** two counterbored holes at the stated centres. Their height and counterbore are user-editable, with a stated default and a visible "assumed, measure your jaw" note. Then a toolpath that machines into the jaw (next point) is collision-checked against the screws.

3. **A nest from the part ("machine the part into the jaws"):** for a second setup, the jaw pair gets a pocket shaped like the part's outline at the grip height, plus a clearance offset, as an operation or a fixture feature. This gives:
   - one project that **cuts the soft jaws** (the jaws are the stock) with an ordinary 2D pocket, refusing corners tighter than the tool radius;
   - a **later setup** that uses the same jaws, with the nest, as its fixture, so the collision check sees the real pocket and not a plain block.

   Today this takes an external CAD model of the nested jaw imported as a model fixture.

## Done means

- The accessory picker offers the presets above by vise size, and Custom asks for L × H × T, bolt centres and screw. Presets load from a data file in `assets/`.
- The jaw model carries its bolt holes and counterbores. A pin shows a nest pocket that would cut into a counterbore being refused by name.
- A soft-jaw nest can be generated from a part's outline (clearance offset, grip depth) and used both as the stock of a jaw-cutting setup and as the fixture of a later setup. A pin shows the later setup's collision check seeing the pocket.
- Each change is an undoable command, with its MCP tool and a structural UI test.

Related: #789 (soft jaw accessory), #339 (fixtures/vises), #1262 (workholding docs, second setups).

body:
Part of #1446 (first slice: the motion-crate generator, `camcraft_motion::machining2d::rest_plan` / `rest_pocket`, on branch `issue/1446-rest-2d`).

Asked for by the maintainer (2026-11-13, quoted on #1446): "We wanna cover some of the toolpaths and things like that at first." and "Lets create issues on your suggestions, they made sense." Sources as he asked: "We should use perplexity to find literature on those types of toolpaths and not copy them straight up".

What the first slice leaves out of the generator, each of which needs design before code:

1. **2D Adaptive over a rest area.** `rest_pocket` refuses the Adaptive strategy by name. The adaptive plan picks its own entry and bounds engagement assuming a full pocket; over a rest area the entry should stand in cleared floor and the engagement model must know what is already cut.
2. **Entry from already-cut space.** The first slice plunges into each rest area like a plain pocket, so nothing depends on the cleared-area estimate. Entering sideways from cleared floor is faster, and makes that estimate safety-critical: the cleared area must be read small (it is today) and the entry refused, by name, where it cannot be proved.
3. **The previous tool from the previous operations.** Today the previous tool is entered by hand and trusted (the path says so in a note). Where the carried stock cannot be established, refuse by name or mark incomplete; never guess.
4. **Zigzag.** Refused by name in the first slice because rows leave cusps along the walls of a rest area. A row plan with a closing ring per rest area would lift the refusal.

Done means: each of the four is either built with its pinning tests (verifier clean, no rapid into material the cleared-area reading cannot prove cut, refusals named) or split into its own issue with a recorded decision; the literature used is cited in the PR.

A 2D drawing (a DXF from a CAD or sheet-metal program) cannot be loaded, so a flat part cannot be profiled without first being modelled as a solid. No DXF code exists in the tree today; issues 743 and 744 want DXF for tool and fixture profiles and can share this reader.

Wanted:
- A DXF reader for the 2D entities that carry a profile: LINE, ARC, CIRCLE, LWPOLYLINE and POLYLINE (with bulges), ELLIPSE and SPLINE (flattened within a tolerance, arcs kept as arcs where they are arcs). Units from `$INSUNITS`, with a question to the user when the file states none (never a silent guess between mm and inch). Layers are kept, so the user can pick by layer. Blocks/INSERT are expanded or refused by name; text, dimensions and hatches are skipped and counted in the import summary.
- The drawing loads as sketch geometry on the setup's XY plane: shown in the viewport, placed with the stock, saved in the project file.
- Chaining: touching entities are joined into chains within a tolerance; closed chains are told from open ones, and outer loops from holes.
- The 2D operations (2D Contour first; Pocket, Slot, Engrave and the plasma/laser profile operations after) take those chains as their geometry selection, with side (inside/outside) and direction per chain, exactly as they take model edges today.
- Loading is an undoable command with its MCP tool (Everything Is a Command; commands ship with an MCP tool). Model > Open offers `.dxf`, and so does the viewport drop of issue 1450.

- The reader is an importer of untrusted files: malformed group codes, truncated files, NaN or huge coordinates, zero-length entities and self-intersecting loops give a clean error or a named skip, never a crash or a hang; it gets a fuzz test like the other importers.
- A gap wider than the chaining tolerance leaves an open chain that is shown as open; it is never closed silently, and an inside/outside cut on an open chain is refused by name.
- A flattened spline or ellipse stays within the stated tolerance of the drawn curve, pinned by a test, so the cut part is to size.
- Units are part of the result: the import summary states them, and a wrong-unit part (25.4 times too big or small) cannot happen without the user having answered the question.

Sources: the DXF format from Autodesk's published DXF reference (a public file-format document; format only), written from scratch or through a permissively licensed crate if one fits (a new dependency needs the maintainer's yes and a `docs/decisions/` entry). No DXF sample files taken from another product's install tree.

Scope note: this is larger than one PR. Suggested split when it is picked up: (1) reader + fuzz test in the geometry crate, (2) sketch entity, project file and viewport display, (3) chaining and selection in 2D Contour, (4) the other 2D operations.

title: Build cycle: every worktree compiles the whole dependency tree cold - share a compile cache, cut debug info, use a faster linker

labels.name: P5
labels.description: Agent surface and tooling keep up with what shipped

body:
Raised by the maintainer (2026-11-11): "why are we cold building complete bundles .. the tests are localized to crates".

## What happens today (measured on the dev machine)
- Every issue worker, reviewer and gate works in its own worktree with its own `target/`. A fresh one compiles the WHOLE dependency tree before the first test runs: about 15-25 minutes per review and 25-75 minutes per gate, almost all of it third-party crates (flecs' C through bindgen/cc, wgpu/egui, the B-rep kernel, the script engine ...), not our code.
- `Cargo.toml` sets `[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 2`: every dependency is optimised in dev builds. That makes tests run faster but makes each cold build much slower.
- Nothing sets `debug`, so dev builds carry full debug info for all crates: one `target/` reaches 50-120 GB (the disk filled twice today) and every link is slow.
- Integration tests are one binary per file: `crates/app/tests` has 266 files, motion 65, sim 50. The batch gate's app step takes about 24 of its 38 minutes, much of it linking and starting 266 binaries.
- `.cargo/config.toml` holds only the `xtask` alias: no linker choice, no cache wrapper. `sccache` is not installed; `rust-lld` is.

## Wanted (this issue: the three cheap ones, measured)
1. **A shared compile cache across worktrees** (`sccache` as `RUSTC_WRAPPER`, and as the C compiler wrapper for the cc-built C code if that works on MSVC). Registry crates live at the same path for every worktree, so their compilations are cache hits; a fresh worktree should then compile only our own crates. It must be OPTIONAL: a machine without sccache builds exactly as today (enable it from `cargo xtask` / the gate wrappers when `sccache` is on PATH, or document the env var - never hard-code a wrapper in `.cargo/config.toml` that breaks a machine without it). Say how to install it and how big its cache is allowed to grow.
2. **Less debug info**: `debug = false` (or `"line-tables-only"`) for dependencies, and line tables only for our crates in dev/test - enough for backtraces and panics with file:line. Report target size and link time before/after.
3. **A faster linker** for the Windows MSVC target (`rust-lld` / `lld-link`), and the equivalent on Linux/macOS where it helps, again without breaking a machine that lacks it.
4. Re-examine `opt-level = 2` for all dependencies: keep it only for the crates whose speed the tests need (measure: batch gate time with opt-level 2 everywhere vs 1 vs a short list).

Measure and report, on the same machine, cold (empty target, warm cache where a cache applies) and warm: `cargo test -p camcraft-app --no-run`, `cargo test -p camcraft-app --test <one binary>`, `cargo xtask gate quick` on a one-file app change, and the `target/` size. No test may change behaviour; the gates stay green.

## Not in this issue (file separately if the numbers say so)
- Folding the 266 one-file app test binaries into a few binaries (one per area, files as modules). This is the biggest structural win for the gate, but it changes the gate maps in `xtask` and every "run this binary" instruction.

## Process
`.cargo/config.toml`, `xtask/` and the gate wrappers are process files: bump `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION`, and say in the PR what a fork must do.

Done means: a fresh worktree reaches its first app test at least 3x faster than today with the cache warm, `target/` is at most half today's size, the settings are optional per machine and documented, and the measured numbers are in the PR.

title: Picking: only feature edges, feature points and faces are pickable, never tessellation edges or hidden geometry - one rule for the whole app

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: source:agent

labels.name: P3

body:
Reported by the maintainer (filed by an agent), 2026-11-10.

## What happens
1. **Tessellation edges are pickable.** The selector lets you pick edges between the mesh's own triangles (at a model's vertices, inside flat faces and along smooth curves). Those aren't real model edges, and no feature should ever be built on them.
2. **Picks go through the model.** In some cases, the "select through" behaviour picks an edge (or a vertex) on the far side of the model, hidden from the user, instead of what's under the cursor.
3. **Inconsistent everywhere.** Face, vertex and edge picking behave differently from page to page: setup alignment, operation geometry, fixture mates, the WCS/origin picks, MCP picks. Users can't build a mental model of what a click will select.

## What should happen - one picking rule, used everywhere
- **Faces:** a face is a welded face, i.e. a smooth patch of triangles merged across soft edges (the `features`/`area` patches MCP's `list_features` already reports). Clicking anywhere on it picks the whole face, never a single triangle.
- **Edges:** only **feature edges** are pickable: edges where two welded faces meet at a real crease, plus open boundary edges of a sheet. Edges between triangles of the same welded face (flat-face triangulation, facets of a smooth cylinder) are never pickable. Chains follow feature edges only.
- **Points:** only **feature points** are pickable: corners where feature edges meet, the end points of open feature-edge chains, and (where a mode asks for it) arc/circle centres derived from a round feature edge. Interior mesh vertices are never pickable.
- **Visible first, never through:** a pick resolves to the front-most visible surface under the cursor (the same depth the viewport draws, perspective and ortho). An edge or point is pickable only if it is visible there (not occluded by the model, within a small screen-space tolerance of the front surface). Nothing on the far side is picked unless the user explicitly turns on a "pick through" mode, which is off by default and shown as such.
- **Snapping order near a feature:** within the pick radius, prefer point, then edge, then face, but **only** among the kinds the current tool accepts (e.g. plane alignment is faces only after #554; axis by edge or two points takes edges/points). A tool that doesn't accept edges never snaps to one.
- **One implementation:** a single picking service in the app layer (feature graph: welded faces, feature edges, feature points; visibility test against the depth the viewport uses) that every UI picker (`plane_pick`, `edge_pick`, `vertex_pick`, `axis_pick`, fixture locate, origin/WCS picks) and the MCP pick tools call. No page carries its own picking rules.

## Done means
- A shared feature-graph and pick API in the app layer, with tests:
  - a flat face's triangulation edges are not pickable;
  - a cylinder's facet edges are not pickable but its circular rim is;
  - a box corner is a pickable point, while a vertex inside a face isn't;
  - a feature edge on the far side of the part is not picked through the near face, in both perspective and ortho;
  - "pick through", when explicitly on, does pick it.
- Every UI picker and the MCP pick tools use it (no local pick logic left); UI tests on the setup page, op geometry and fixture locate confirm the behaviour.
- A short note in the user docs (#688) on what a click picks.

Related: #554 (plane picks faces only), #557 (axis by edge/points), #555 (three points), #561/#566 (fixture locate), #180 (MCP picks), #241 (selecting on complex planar faces), #613/#609/#610 (ortho rays).

title: Process changes - fork maintainers please subscribe

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: P?
labels.description: Paused: never picked until the maintainer sets a real priority

body:
**Subscribe to this issue** (the "Subscribe" button on the right) if you work from a fork of CamCraft, especially with an AI agent.

Forks sync product code only at release tags (AGENTS.md "A fork syncs from upstream at each cut tag"). But the *process* - `AGENTS.md`, the agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, the skills in `.claude/skills/` and `scripts/gate.*` - changes between releases, and a fork's agents should follow the current rules (review labels, priority labels, release steps, and so on).

**How it works:**
- `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one number. Every PR that changes a process file bumps it.
- Every such PR also adds a comment **here**: the new version, what changed, and what to pull. Subscribers get one notification per change.
- A fork's agent compares its `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` with upstream's at the start of each session and, if upstream is newer, pulls just the process files (AGENTS.md "Process files sync on every session"). Product code still waits for the next release tag.

**To pull by hand:**
```
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/main -- AGENTS.md .claude/agents .claude/skills .claude/PROCESS_VERSION scripts/gate.ps1 scripts/gate.sh
git commit -m "chore(process): sync process files to upstream PROCESS_VERSION <n>"
```

This issue stays open and pinned. It's labelled `P?` so no agent ever picks it up as work.

body:
Reported by a user (relayed in chat, 2026-11-07); filed by an agent.

**Setup**: laptop with a dual-GPU setup - Intel UHD (integrated) + NVIDIA Quadro P3200 (discrete), Windows.

**What happens**
1. With both GPUs enabled, the app rejects / ends up on the Intel UHD adapter and **never renders** (no viewport).
2. With the Intel GPU turned off, the NVIDIA chip **does not pick up the work** either.
3. When the app is connected to the Quadro P3200, the UI **lags 1-2 s** just rotating the empty plane view (no model loaded).

**Expected**: the app picks a working adapter (preferring the discrete GPU on hybrid systems), renders, and orbiting an empty scene is smooth on a P3200.

**Where to look** (from a read of the code, not yet reproduced):
- `crates/ui/src/egui_app/shell.rs` ~231-252: `RequestAdapterOptions { compatible_surface, ..Default::default() }` - `power_preference` is left at the default, and there is no adapter enumeration or choice by vendor/device; the fallback chain (`gpu.rs` `attempts`, `GpuPick`) only varies the *backend* (DX12 -> PRIMARY -> all), never the adapter. On Optimus/hybrid laptops the surface is presented by the integrated GPU, so a discrete adapter may not be `compatible_surface`, and the default pick can land on the Intel adapter.
- When an adapter is found but rendering never starts, there is no named refusal visible to the user - check `self.fail(...)` paths after `request_device` and surface configure (format/present-mode on the Intel adapter).
- The 1-2 s lag on an empty scene suggests a per-frame stall: present mode / vsync with a cross-adapter copy (discrete renders, iGPU presents), a blocking readback (`pollster::block_on` or a map_async wait) in the frame loop, or redraw driven by a timeout instead of input.

**Done means**
- The app enumerates adapters and logs every one it sees (name, vendor, backend, device type) at startup; the chosen one is printed by `gpu::describe(...).log_line()` already.
- On a hybrid Intel+NVIDIA laptop it renders on either GPU: prefer `PowerPreference::HighPerformance` (or a user setting to pick the adapter by name), and fall back adapter-by-adapter, not only backend-by-backend, refusing by name only when none works.
- Orbiting an empty scene on the P3200 runs at display rate (no multi-second frames); the frame-time cause is found and pinned by a test or a logged frame-time budget.

**Needs from the reporter**: the app's startup GPU log line(s) (the `gpu:` lines on stdout/stderr), Windows "Graphics settings" per-app GPU preference, NVIDIA Control Panel preferred-GPU setting, and driver versions for both GPUs.
